news.content: NVIDIA announced a record-breaking 104-qubit simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum processor, performed on the JUPITER supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre using NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. The company stated this advancement aims to accelerate the development of useful quantum applications in areas such as drug discovery, financial modeling, and materials science.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) has become a warning signal for the debt-financed side of the AI boom, according to one credit expert.

"CoreWeave is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment coming under more stress, said Max Frumes, 9fin global head of distressed and leveraged finance at corporate credit data and analytics firm, Reuters reported.

Frumes expects other AI-linked debt to follow CoreWeave into distressed territory. 

"This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that’s supporting the AI boom," he said. "It’s going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors."

  • CRWV stock is moving. See the real-time price action here. 

Bonds Flash Distress

His comments come after a brutal stretch for the AI cloud provider. The yield on CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds jumped above 16% last week, beyond the level generally associated with distress, Reuters reported. 

The company has piled up more than $51 billion in debt and obligations to fund its AI infrastructure expansion.

Insurance against a default got pricier, too. The cost of protecting CoreWeave’s debt climbed above 1,000 basis points to record highs, according to Reuters.

The stock took a beating. Shares dropped more than 11% on Friday, bringing weekly losses close to 25%, per Benzinga Pro data.

A hot inflation reading contributed to the sell-off because CoreWeave’s model amounts to a heavily indebted bet on future data center demand.

Read Also: We Asked ChatGPT, Grok and Claude For 1 Stock to Buy This Week. No One Picked Tesla.

Retail Traders Buy the Dip

Retail investors saw opportunity in the wreckage. Customers of Robinhood Markets Inc. (NASDAQ:HOOD) logged their biggest week of net CoreWeave purchases on record as the stock shed about a quarter of its value, according to Robinhood data.

CoreWeave also ranked as the third-most purchased single security on the platform Friday, behind only Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies Inc (NASDAQ:SPCX). 

Notably, CEO Elon Musk, who leads both companies, stoked credit fears last week when he replied "yikes" on social media to a post about the surging yields on CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Neoclouds Feel the Heat

CoreWeave sits at the front of a group of newer providers known as neoclouds, which rent out scarce and expensive processors from NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and frequently borrow to pay for the chips. 

Rivals such as Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS), Applied Digital Corp. (NASDAQ:APLD) and IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN) also tumbled during the rout. 

CoreWeave pushed back in an internal memo: CEO Mike Intrator told employees the company’s backlog more than covers its debt obligations and argued markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally." 

Co-founder Brannin McBee has said the company is pursuing an investment-grade rating.

Some market watchers see the sell-off as a CoreWeave-specific problem. Tommaso Leodari, chief investment officer at Dubai-based hedge fund Index & Cie, told Reuters the company should not be treated as the poster child for AI.  

Frumes sees a wider reckoning. If he is right, the cheap and plentiful credit behind the AI build-out is about to get scarcer. Borrowers will pay more, and lenders will ask tougher questions.

Key Takeaways

  • The 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) yield closed at 2.78% on Oct. 15, up from 1.71% a year earlier, yet the S&P 500 gained 16.8% in that span.
  • The index’s forward P/E fell to 19.0 from 22.4 while forward earnings estimates rose about 38%. Earnings carried the gain.
  • With the earnings yield about 2.5 points above TIPS, each quarter-point rise in real yields is worth roughly 4.5% of index value if estimates stay flat.

On Sept. 17, the morning after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate for the first time since 2023, the Treasury sold $19 billion of 10-year TIPS at a real yield of 2.653%, the highest for that maturity at auction since October 2008. In theory, that should make stocks harder to own.

But the S&P 500 closed at 7,744.06 on Oct. 15, up 16.8% from a year earlier per FRED index data, even as the 10-year real yield rose from 1.71% to 2.78%, near its highest level since the 2008 financial crisis. Did stock investors ignore the bond market? The arithmetic says no.

The Multiple Shrank 15% And The Index Still Rose 17%

An index price is two numbers multiplied together. One is expected earnings per share; the other is the multiple investors pay for them, and separating them shows a textbook repricing that earnings outran.

FactSet’s Oct. 17, 2025 report put the S&P 500’s forward 12-month P/E at 22.4. Its latest Earnings Insight, dated Oct. 16, 2026, puts it at 19.0, below its five-year average of 19.8.

Dividing price by multiple implies forward earnings of about $296 a share a year ago and $408 now, and a 15% smaller multiple applied to 38% more earnings produces almost exactly the 17% price gain. Rates did bite. The earnings boom bit harder.

Chris Carpentier, a senior investment strategist at State Street Investment Management, reached the same conclusion in a Sept. 21 note. “Markets are still responding to higher discount rates in a manner broadly consistent with financial theory,” he wrote.

Two Measures Of The Cushion Point Different Ways

The equity risk premium (ERP) is the extra annual return investors demand for holding stocks instead of a risk-free bond, and when it runs thin, a modest rate shock can erase months of gains. Nobody observes it directly.

The simplest estimate subtracts the real yield from the forward earnings yield, the inverse of the P/E. At 19.0 times earnings, that yield is 5.26%, or 2.48 percentage points above the TIPS yield, compared with 2.75 points a year earlier, when real yields were more than a full point lower. The cushion narrowed by 0.27.

Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at NYU Stern, gets a different reading from his cash-flow model. His implied ERP series rose to 4.20% on Oct. 1 from 3.78% a year earlier, even as the Treasury rate he uses climbed to 5.29% from 4.16%. His trailing cash-yield version slipped to 3.70% from 4.01%, closer to Carpentier’s view that the premium “has compressed and remains at lows.”

Forward-earnings measures depend on analysts being right, and cash-yield measures assume the past year repeats; neither shows stocks as cheap relative to TIPS. The method decides the answer.

Two Chipmakers Carry 9 Points Of Earnings Growth

The earnings lift is narrow. FactSet’s blended third-quarter growth rate is 29.0%, but exclude Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) and NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and it falls to 20.0%.

Growth should slow. FactSet consensus projects 16.0% for calendar 2027 but only 2.8% for the second quarter of 2027 as year-ago comparisons stiffen, while sector multiples range from 13.3 times forward earnings for Energy to 23.4 for Consumer Discretionary.

The sensitivity is steep. Hold the 2.48-point cushion constant and leave earnings estimates flat, and a quarter-point rise in the real yield implies a P/E near 18.1, or about 4.5% lower prices. A half-point rise implies roughly 17.4 times earnings, an 8.7% decline, while a half-point drop supports about 21 times.

A Quarter-Point Hike Does Not Reopen Hormuz

CBS reporter Richard Escobedo put the problem plainly at the Sept. 16 press conference. A quarter-point hike, he told Chair Kevin Warsh, “does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz.” Warsh replied that the Fed “cannot affect any individual price” but can keep relative price changes from broadening, the official transcript shows.

The September CPI report shows the gap. Headline inflation hit 3.7%, with gasoline up 34.2% over 12 months, while core ran at 2.6%. Regular gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in the week of Oct. 12, up from $3.06 a year earlier, EIA weekly data show, and the CPI print briefly lifted rate-hike bets, Benzinga reported.

The bond market is pricing the shock as temporary. The 10-year breakeven rate, the inflation rate at which TIPS and ordinary Treasuries of the same maturity return the same, stood at 2.35% on Oct. 16, next to the Fed’s median projection of 2.3% inflation for 2027 on its preferred PCE gauge.

Warsh listed this among the Fed’s aims: ensuring “that inflation compensation in market prices stays low.” For investors, that sets the bar. TIPS beat nominal 10-year Treasuries only if inflation averages more than about 2.35% over the decade, and Warsh noted that inflation has run above target for more than five years.

Inflation protection is not price protection. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF (NYSE:TIP) shows a 2.81% real yield and a 6.19-year effective duration, yet its net asset value total return was negative 0.95% year to date as of Oct. 15. Real yields rose 0.84 points this year, and that duration implies roughly a 6% price loss per full point.

What The 2.8% Hurdle Means For A Portfolio

A risk-free real return near 2.8% now sets the bar for every risk asset, and stocks clear it by a narrower margin than a year ago.

  • Measure stocks against the real yield. The forward earnings yield minus the 10-year TIPS yield, now 2.48 points, is a workable cushion gauge; FactSet’s weekly revisions show which way it is moving.
  • Match the instrument to the date. Individual TIPS held to maturity lock in their real yield; a fund such as TIP never matures, so its price moves with real yields. Under TreasuryDirect rules, principal changes may affect federal taxes yearly, so account location matters.
  • Check allocation drift. A stock-and-TIPS mix set a year ago, such as one built with the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and TIP, has likely drifted toward stocks. Written rebalancing bands decide when drift becomes a trade.
  • Watch the next catalysts. FactSet lists Oct. 21 for the first “Magnificent 7” reports, and the Federal Open Market Committee meets Oct. 27-28. Prediction-market traders put October hike odds at 14%.

Equities absorbed higher real yields because earnings grew faster than the discount rate rose; if that reverses, the earnings line will show it first. Stocks now compete with a specific number.

At the Oct. 15 real yield, $100,000 placed in a 10-year TIPS and held to maturity compounds to about $131,500 in today’s purchasing power, before taxes.

NVIDIA Corp’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) biggest advantage in AI is not just the chips it sells. It is CUDA, the software ecosystem developers rely on to build and run AI workloads.

Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) may have found a way to challenge that advantage by making it easier for developers to use its own AI chips without rewriting their code.

Amazon introduced TorchNeuron, an open-source tool designed to run PyTorch-based AI code on its Trainium chips with minimal modifications. The move targets one of the biggest barriers to switching from Nvidia: the engineering time and expense involved in adapting software to a different computing platform.

• NVIDIA shares are advancing steadily. What’s driving NVDA shares up?

Amazon Targets CUDA’s Advantage

Nvidia’s software ecosystem creates switching costs that extend beyond hardware performance. Developers have spent years building workflows around CUDA, making it difficult for competing chips to win workloads even when they offer attractive economics.

Amazon is trying to lower that hurdle. According to its TorchNeuron announcement, developers can run existing PyTorch code on Trainium with a configuration change rather than rewriting entire applications.

That matters because PyTorch is widely used across AI research and development. Amazon does not need to displace CUDA immediately; it needs to make experimenting with an alternative less costly and time-consuming.

Trainium’s Bigger Opportunity

The launch builds on Amazon’s effort to expand its custom silicon business across AI training and inference. Its Trainium accelerators give Amazon Web Services a way to offer computing capacity built around its own hardware rather than relying entirely on Nvidia GPUs.

Amazon’s custom chips have attracted major AI customers, including Anthropic, which uses Trainium in its Project Rainier computing cluster. TorchNeuron could make the platform accessible to more developers who might otherwise stick with Nvidia because switching involves too much work.

Amazon has said more than 30 early customers across fields including robotics, voice AI and world models are using the tool. Broader adoption could help AWS compete on both computing costs and the ease of deploying AI applications.

Read Also: Nvidia’s AI Boom Has a Hidden Dependency: One Dutch Company

What It Means for Nvidia

The announcement does not mean Nvidia’s lead is about to disappear. CUDA remains a mature ecosystem, and Amazon still has to prove that Trainium delivers competitive performance, reliability and economics across demanding workloads.

But the competitive pressure could grow if developers can move applications between platforms with fewer changes. That would give cloud customers more flexibility and potentially strengthen Amazon’s bargaining power on AI infrastructure costs.

For investors, the key question is whether Amazon can turn easier software migration into sustained Trainium demand. Amazon is not just trying to build an alternative to Nvidia’s chips; it is trying to reduce the software friction that keeps customers tied to them. If it succeeds, Nvidia’s moat may become less difficult to cross.

Investor Steve Eisman states that Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) faces “concentration risk” because five customers account for 70% of the company’s accounts receivable, based on data from its recent 10-Q filing.

Concentration Risk in AI

Eisman, a former Frontpoint partner, discussed his outlook on the artificial intelligence sector with former partner Danny Moses on an episode of “The Real Eisman Playbook” podcast.

During the discussion, Eisman clarified his stance on the sector, stating, “I’m not going out telling people to short the whole AI trade. I think that would be insane.” However, he specified that “one of the things that work concerns me is the concentration risk.”

Read Also: The Moment Jensen Huang Realized Nvidia 'Won't Have to Die' Came After a Call From This CEO: 'For the Whole Time, 30 Years…'

Nvidia’s 10-Q Filing Data

Eisman noted that while Nvidia recently reported a 106% revenue increase, the company’s subsequent 10-Q filing showed “that 70% of Nvidia’s accounts receivable is from five accounts.”

According to Nvidia’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended July 26, five unnamed direct customers accounted for 22%, 14%, 13%, 11%, and 10% of the accounts receivable balance.

To illustrate his point, Eisman recounted a story about a former software analyst who refused to take a fast-growing company public because it relied on only three customers.

Comparing this to Nvidia, Eisman stated, “Nvidia is the largest company in the world and 70% of its of its revenue comes from five customers.” He concluded by reiterating, “There’s a lot of there’s just a tremendous amount of concentration risk.”

Broader Industry Reliance

Beyond Nvidia’s specific customer concentration, Eisman expressed concern regarding the broader artificial intelligence sector’s dependence on specific private firms.

He stated that “so much of this whole chain is dependent upon the health of OpenAI and Anthropic.” Eisman added that it is impossible to handicap this reliance because “we don’t even have any financials at this point.”

Moses added that the reliance on AI growth is a “national security issue in the sense of the economy,” noting that it contributes a massive amount of growth to GDP.

AI data center stocks bounced back on Monday after taking a beating last week, but "Mad Money" host Jim Cramer says investors should not rush to call a bottom. With major hyperscalers set to report earnings, Cramer is looking for several signs before becoming bullish on the battered group.

AI Data Center Stocks Need To Prove The Rebound Is Real, Says Cramer

Cramer said the first hurdle is technical. AI data center stocks have produced ugly chart patterns after peaking in June, including potential double tops in semiconductor and memory ETFs and head-and-shoulders formations in other parts of the group.

"The charts need to get better," Cramer said.

Monday’s rebound was encouraging, but Cramer wants to see a stronger move that establishes a pattern of "higher highs and higher lows." He also pointed out that last week’s selloff did not break the late-July lows, which marked the bottom of the previous major wave of AI data center selling.

"Today’s bounce though, I’m going to call it a good start," he said.

Read Also: Chevron, ExxonMobil Stocks Hit 52-Week Highs as Fresh US-Israel Threats Against Iran Push Brent Crude to 5-Month Highs

The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq-100 also fell below their 50-day moving averages during Friday’s selloff. Cramer said getting back above those levels would provide another important signal that the group is stabilizing.

Until then, investors should be careful about treating Monday’s rebound as a confirmed turnaround.

Microsoft, Alphabet And Amazon Earnings Could Make Or Break The Trade

The next major test comes from the hyperscalers. Cramer said earnings from companies spending enormous sums on AI infrastructure will reveal whether the spending boom remains intact.

"If you’re hoping for a resurgence in the AI data center cohort, these companies need to maintain their gigantic capital spending spree," Cramer said. "Need to maintain, not cut."

Any indication that Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) or Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) are preparing to slow their AI investments could quickly hit the broader data center trade.

"If they start to signal that they’re preparing to dial back their investments, the whole group is going to get whacked," Cramer said. He added that investors will also be watching whether that spending is translating into actual cloud and data center revenue.

"We need to see that they believe in it," Cramer said, pointing to the potential for "hundreds of billions of dollars in revenues."

Cramer expects the upcoming earnings stretch to be a "high stakes gauntlet of tech earnings." Strong cloud infrastructure growth combined with continued capital spending could help restore confidence in AI data center stocks.

"As long as they don’t blink, though, I think we can get through this," he said.

Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon are set to report their latest quarterly results next week. Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) will report its results on Wednesday, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Midterm Elections And Anthropic IPO Could Provide Final Confirmation

Cramer sees two more potential catalysts before investors can confidently declare a bottom: the U.S. midterm elections and a potential Anthropic IPO.

"I don’t think the AI data center cohort can put in a sustainable bottom until after the midterm election," Cramer said.

He argued that data centers have become politically sensitive ahead of the election, creating uncertainty for companies planning major projects. Once the election is over, Cramer believes state and local officials may be more willing to negotiate with hyperscalers over new data center investments.

The potential Anthropic IPO could offer another important test of the AI spending cycle. "We need to see someone is making money or will soon be making money from all this data center investment," Cramer said.

A successful IPO could give investors more confidence that AI infrastructure spending ultimately leads to sustainable profits.

For now, however, Cramer remains cautious. "Even after today’s bounce, I still think it’s just a little too early to say that the coast is clear and it’s safe to dive back into the hardest-hit AI data center stocks," he said.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock fell more than 3% in Tuesday’s premarket trading as concerns over the AI cloud provider’s rising borrowing costs and heavy debt continued to weigh on investor sentiment.

The decline came amid broader market weakness, with Nasdaq futures down 0.37% and S&P 500 futures slipping 0.04%.

Despite strong demand for AI computing infrastructure and renewed optimism from Wall Street analysts, CoreWeave has struggled to rebound from a sharp selloff. The stock is down nearly 15% year to date.

Evercore Sees Strong AI Demand Despite Debt Concerns

Evercore ISI Senior Managing Director Amit Daryanani maintained an Outperform rating and a $150 price forecast on CoreWeave.

Daryanani told CNBC on Monday that investors were focusing heavily on a relatively small portion of unsecured debt yielding 14% to 15%.

He said much of CoreWeave’s debt is backed by contracts with high-credit-quality customers, including Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and OpenAI. Those arrangements carry financing costs of about 5.5%.

He also noted that GPU rental prices rose 15% to 20% per quarter over the past two quarters.

Meanwhile, some recent CoreWeave contracts generated approximately $20 million in annual revenue per megawatt, compared with a historical range of $10 million to $11 million.

Evercore estimates that CoreWeave can generate returns on invested capital of 15% to 20% per project.

Daryanani believes a 100- to 200-basis-point increase in borrowing costs would remain manageable. However, financing all future projects at 15% would pose a significant challenge.

Goldman Sachs Sees Upside Despite Financing Concerns

On Monday, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges upgraded CoreWeave to Buy from Neutral but lowered the price forecast to $106 from $139.

Borges said investors may be overestimating CoreWeave’s future borrowing costs while overlooking potential improvements in returns.

The analyst noted that CoreWeave had raised computing prices by 25% in July and another 10% in October, reflecting strong demand for AI infrastructure.

However, Goldman Sachs warned that financing costs and shifts in AI computing demand remain key risks.

Meanwhile, the yield on CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds fell to 15.13% from more than 16% last week, according to Tradeweb data cited by Reuters.

However, Great Hill Capital Chairman Thomas Hayes warned that bond investors remain skeptical and could demand higher yields to finance AI infrastructure growth.

According to Bloomberg, credit investors are raising concerns about the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure as a wave of new debt issuance approaches.

Meanwhile, John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, said the bigger concern is the substantial debt supply expected over the next 18 months.

He added that companies’ willingness to pay increasingly higher borrowing costs could hurt existing bondholders, making investors reluctant to buy debt before yields rise further.

The KBW Nasdaq Bank Index, which tracks 24 of the largest U.S. lenders, has fallen for six straight weeks — its longest losing run since July 2008. It slipped another 1.1% on Monday, putting it on track for a seventh.

The index closed Monday at 167.15 points. That is 11.8% below where it stood when the streak began in early September, and 13.8% below its Aug. 14 record close of 193.91.

Bank stocks are now up just 1.8% this year, against an 11.8% gain for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY).

Read Also: Chip Stocks Repeated a Lehman-Era Losing Streak: Is The Bottom Now In?

Memories of 2008

In the spring and summer of 2008, U.S. bank stocks fell for 10 weeks in a row. Bear Stearns had already been rescued. Lehman Brothers would file for bankruptcy two months after the streak ended.

In the 18 years since, bank stocks have never lost more than five weeks in a row. That record has now been broken.

Last month, the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time since 2023 to 3.75% to 4.00%.

Long-term yields followed. The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.12%, the 30-year at 5.45% and the 2-year at 4.77%.

Higher rates can help banks earn more on loans. When they rise quickly, however, they cut the value of the bonds banks already own and raise the risk that borrowers fall behind on payments.

Investors appear to be trading bank stocks against the direction of rates, treating a rapid climb as a clear negative, according to a Bank of America Global Research report led by analyst Ebrahim Poonawala.

Bank Of America Takes The Biggest Hit

Bank of America Corp. (NYSE:BAC) reported a few days after the Treasury Department hit it with a $1.2 billion penalty. Regulators found the bank failed to properly report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions.

Third-quarter net income fell to $6.9 billion from $8.3 billion a year earlier. Trading revenue dropped 5% and investment banking fees 11%.

The stock trades at $50.39, about 23% below its 2026 high.

Citigroup Inc. (NYSE:C) sits 18% below its June peak. Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) has lost 11.7% over the past month.

Bank of America does not read the selloff as a verdict on profits.

“Positioning, not fundamentals or EPS revisions, drove post-earnings stock reactions,” Poonawala said in the report.

The bank saw no material change to 2027 earnings estimates. Large U.S. banks trade at about 10 times expected 2027 earnings, according to the report.

Read Also: Nasdaq 100 Stocks Add Nearly $500 Billion As Chips Battle To Snap 2008-Style Rout

Not One Bank In The Index Is Above Its 50-Day Average

None of the 24 stocks in the KBW index trades above its 50-day moving average, the average closing price of the past 50 sessions, Jonathan Roque of 22V Research said in a note on Monday. Only 29% are above their 200-day average.

Roque flagged six names that together make up half of the index’s market value: Bank of America, Capital One Financial Corp. (NYSE:COF), Citigroup, Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC), Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS).

All six trade below both averages.

Rouge sees the index risking a drop to its March low, near 146 to 147 points.

“The market cannot go up when banks go down,” Roque said.

Regional lenders have held up better. The State Street SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (NYSE:KRE) is up 6.7% this year.

The comparison with 2008 has limits. Back then, the streak reflected mounting losses on mortgage assets.

This time, Bank of America links the pressure to rising rates and investor positioning, not to the banks’ earnings.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) shares closed at $61.39 on Monday, about 56% below their 52-week high of $139.93. HSBC sees more downside ahead for the AI cloud provider.

HSBC analysts maintained a Reduce rating and a $39 price target in a note published Monday. The target implies 36.5% downside from Monday’s close. The firm left its non-GAAP earnings estimates unchanged, and those forecasts remain far below Wall Street consensus.

  • CRWV stock is sinking. See the chart and price action here. 

Neocloud Model Under Pressure

HSBC argues CoreWeave faces structural disadvantages against hyperscalers. The firm expects CoreWeave to generate about $12 million in annual revenue per megawatt in 2027, compared with $17 million to $18 million for hyperscalers.

Large cloud providers rent capacity under more lucrative short-term contracts, according to the note. They also run differentiated general-purpose cloud businesses and serve many smaller customers who buy the full technology stack. 

Neoclouds, by contrast, earn most of their revenue from large customers renting commoditized bare-metal GPU instances.

Read Also: We Asked ChatGPT, Grok and Claude For 1 Stock to Buy This Week. No One Picked Tesla.

Short-Term Contract Boom Could Fade

Between May and September, neocloud operators signed several lucrative short-term deals. CoreWeave signed three- to six-month contracts in September at roughly $40 million per megawatt annually, HSBC said.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) also struck deals with Anthropic and Alphabet Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google worth an estimated $22 million to $50 million per megawatt each year.

HSBC now sees risks to the trend. Growth among LLM providers has slowed slightly, which could soften demand for spot compute capacity. Rising yields and debt market strain could also stop neoclouds from building speculative capacity, the kind typically offered under those high-priced short-term contracts.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

Estimates Far Below Consensus

HSBC’s non-GAAP EPS estimates for 2028 through 2030 sit 50% to 70% below consensus. Over the long term, the firm expects CoreWeave to post a non-GAAP operating margin of 15% to 16%, while management has guided for about 25%.

Debt Fears Deepen

CoreWeave lost roughly a quarter of its value last week as investors questioned how it would finance its AI buildout, and the slide continues. Shares fell 4.16% to $58.58 in Tuesday premarket trading, a new 52-week low, per Benzinga Pro data. 

Bulls Push Back

Other analysts see the selloff as overdone. Goldman Sachs upgraded CoreWeave to Buy from Neutral on Monday, though it cut its price target to $106 from $139. Analyst Gabriela Borges said investors may be overestimating the company’s future borrowing costs.

Evercore ISI maintained an Outperform rating and a $150 target. Senior Managing Director Amit Daryanani told CNBC much of CoreWeave’s debt is backed by contracts with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and OpenAI. 

HSBC’s $39 target sits far below both.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) reports third-quarter earnings after the bell Tuesday, with its call at 4:30 p.m. ET.

Analysts expect earnings of 14 cents a share on $12.74 billion in revenue, up 63% from last quarter. SpaceX shares plunged nearly 14% after its previous earnings beat.

On Kalshi, traders are betting on what CEO Elon Musk and his team will say. AI terms crowd the top of the board, while a possible Tesla merger adds intrigue.

What Kalshi Predicts SpaceX Will Say

“Starlink” leads at 99%, with “Starship” at 98%. SpaceX ended June with 12 million Starlink subscribers; analysts project another 1.5 million to 1.8 million additions this quarter.

“Grok” trades at 97%, “Cursor” at 96% and “Data Center” at 93%. SpaceX rents out computing power from its Colossus data centers, with new cloud deals adding $1.6 billion in second-quarter revenue, nearly two-thirds of its AI division’s total.

The company signed $14.1 billion in cloud-services contracts. CFO Bret Johnsen said new compute investments pay back in under a year, although the AI division posted a $1.26 billion operating loss. SpaceX bought Cursor for $60 billion in August.

“Moon” sits at 84%. NASA targets a crewed lunar landing in 2028, giving SpaceX a nearer-term deadline than Musk’s Mars ambitions.

“Starmind” trades at 81%, “Colossus” at 78% and “Nvidia” at 74%. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is helping design orbital AI computers based on its Vera Rubin technology, while SpaceX’s terrestrial AI computing capacity reached 1.4 gigawatts in June.

What Kalshi Predicts SpaceX Will Skip

“Mars” trades at 38% and “Artemis,” NASA’s lunar program, at 36%. Traders expect the Moon to come up, but not necessarily by program name, and they’re skeptical Musk pivots to Mars.

“Tesla” trades at 59%, down 25 points, while “Combine / Combining” sits at just 24%.

RBC Capital Markets modeled a hypothetical takeover of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) at $480 a share, creating a $3.74 trillion company. RBC says it knows of no actual deal. Tesla reports Wednesday.

“Starshield” sits at just 15%, days after restrictions disrupted Ukrainian drone operations. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House, while Musk said the U.S. government controls the military satellite system. Four U.S. senators demanded answers from SpaceX on Monday.

“T-Mobile” sits at just 8%. The carrier currently partners with SpaceX to provide satellite phone coverage, but Musk’s company has agreed to buy $8 billion in wireless spectrum previously owned by T-Mobile. The deal could help SpaceX build its own mobile network and compete directly with its partner.

Reading the Board

Musk has promised a $100 billion annualized revenue pace by December, counting on new contracts to rent out AI computing power. That would require nearly doubling monthly sales from the third-quarter average.

But spending worries investors. SpaceX poured $18.4 billion into capital projects last quarter, mostly AI data centers, and analysts expect nearly $19 billion more this quarter. Shares plunged after the last earnings beat as investors questioned whether the returns could justify the mounting costs.
